cards.title: Active Reading
cards.prompt: What are the three gates in the active-reading protocol?
cards.answer: Before: scan and activate a schema. During: do not advance without a section summary. After: retrieve without looking, then compare and target the gaps.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What are protest behaviours?
cards.answer: Escalations — calling more, pushing for the conversation, becoming accusatory — that attempt to re-establish a connection by making its absence more costly to maintain. The intensity is a reconnection strategy, not an attack.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What can heartbreak specifically disprove for an anxiously attached person?
cards.answer: The nervous system’s core prediction. The abandonment it has spent a lifetime preventing actually happens and is survived, which is direct evidence against the belief that made the vigilance necessary.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What is the bind inside anxious reassurance-seeking?
cards.answer: The need is real and urgent, and asking for it is itself an exposure that could trigger the withdrawal being feared. The only direct route to relief runs through the risk it is trying to avoid.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why can a secure partner feel like less love than an inconsistent one?
cards.answer: Because activation is being read as depth of feeling. A reliable partner produces little prediction error and so little activation, and a nervous system trained on uncertain closeness interprets that calm as the absence of love.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why does a small tension trigger a response three levels above it?
cards.answer: The reaction is not to the current moment. The amygdala has matched it against every previous occasion that this kind of tension preceded abandonment, and fired at the weight of the whole set.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why is anxious hypervigilance a rational strategy rather than a distortion?
cards.answer: The threat-detection system is pattern-matching accurately against its own history. In that history, those small signals genuinely did precede withdrawal — the system is doing exactly the job it was trained for.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: In the pursue-withdraw conflict pattern, what do the two roles have in common?
cards.answer: Both are frightened. The escalation and the withdrawal are two different fear-management strategies learned in two different childhood environments, not a difference in how much either person cares.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What does it indicate when someone hears criticism of an action as a verdict on their worth?
cards.answer: A history of conditional love, where what you did was who you were. The behaviour and the person were never separated, so a comment on one still lands as a judgement on the other.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What internal model does secure attachment install?
cards.answer: That others are basically trustworthy and the self is basically worthy of care. Nothing has to be performed to earn love and nothing has to be braced against, which is what produces the ease others find confusing.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What is the "impossible bind" behind disorganized attachment?
cards.answer: The caregiver was both the source of comfort and the source of fear. The attachment system drives toward them for safety while the threat system drives away, and no coherent strategy can satisfy both.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: Why can a self-aware adult still collapse into a childhood pattern under pressure?
cards.answer: Timing. The limbic attachment circuitry fires faster than the prefrontal cortex, so under real emotional stakes the response is already running by the time the deliberate mind gets to evaluate it.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: Why does inconsistent caregiving produce a different pattern than consistently cold caregiving?
cards.answer: Consistent unavailability teaches the child to stop expecting a response at all. Inconsistency teaches that the attachment is winnable but unpredictable, so the child develops continuous monitoring instead of shutdown.

cards.title: Attention–Retention Gap
cards.prompt: What does the attention–retention gap measure that screen time alone misses?
cards.answer: Whether spent attention left anything retrievable, actionable, deliberately restorative, or chosen. Equal minutes can produce very different retained value.

cards.title: Audience Fragmentation
cards.prompt: Why is audience fragmentation more costly than ordinary role variation?
cards.answer: Each audience supplies a quantified optimisation target that must be monitored and adjusted. The issue is not having roles; it is letting several external scoreboards compete to define the underlying preference.

cards.title: Avoidance–Relief Loop
cards.prompt: What reward keeps avoidance repeating?
cards.answer: Immediate relief. When withdrawal makes arousal stop, the system learns that escape produced safety and approaches the next similar cue with still less evidence of its own capacity.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What are deactivating strategies, and when do they fire?
cards.answer: Withdrawal, suddenly noticing the partner’s flaws, idealising singlehood, picking distance-creating fights — and they fire precisely as intimacy deepens, because that is when the nervous system registers threat.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What lesson installs avoidant attachment?
cards.answer: That needing someone leads to pain. The nervous system’s solution is to stop needing — suppress the vulnerability, build a self-sufficient internal world, and hold people at a functional distance.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What separates the dismissive avoidant from the fearful avoidant?
cards.answer: The dismissive holds a high self-view and low other-view and genuinely deactivates the need — rarely in conscious distress. The fearful wants connection intensely and fears it simultaneously, oscillating between both patterns.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: Why does pushing an avoidant for closeness make the distance worse?
cards.answer: Pressure is read as threat, and threat is what triggered the deactivation in the first place. What calms the system is predictable low-pressure presence — safety without urgency.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: Why is avoidant self-sufficiency expensive rather than easy?
cards.answer: Because the relationship cannot be used as a regulation resource. Where secure attachment turns toward the partner under stress, the avoidant must self-regulate alone — which looks like coldness and is actually a high-maintenance internal process.

cards.title: Body Composition
cards.prompt: What do the two halves of body composition each signal?
cards.answer: Low body fat reports metabolic health and physical capability; adequate muscle mass reports testosterone-driven fitness. They are separate readouts, which is why either alone is incomplete.

cards.title: Byproduct Signaling
cards.prompt: What changes when a trait moves from a byproduct signal to a goal signal?
cards.answer: The observer’s account of what the trait points to changes. The trait itself does not reveal whether the account, the motive, or the claimed capability is true.

cards.title: Calibrated Self-Interest
cards.prompt: What calibrates healthy self-interest?
cards.answer: Empathy and reciprocity. Self-respect, pride, and ambition remain healthy when they do not require another person to be diminished, exploited, or made responsible for stabilizing one’s worth.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: How can two people both love genuinely and consistently miss each other?
cards.answer: Because each loves the way they were loved, or the way they wished they had been. Two histories produce two grammars, and neither is failing to give — they are giving in a form the other was not taught to receive.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: What does parentification produce in adulthood?
cards.answer: Inverted boundaries that never righted — compulsive caretaking, an inability to receive care without guilt, and relationships in which the person is permanently the helper.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why does the birth-to-seven window carry disproportionate weight?
cards.answer: Plasticity is unusually high, theta activity dominates, and critical filtering is minimal. The environment is absorbed without the capacity to evaluate or reject it, and the encodings are body-level rather than intellectual.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why is awareness necessary but not sufficient here?
cards.answer: The patterns are encoded in the nervous system rather than the intellect. Naming one removes its automatic quality, but changing it needs somatic awareness and corrective relational experience, not insight alone.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why is the inheritance framing offered as mechanism rather than blame?
cards.answer: Because most parents are transmitting what they themselves received, without having examined its origin. The wound is generational, so locating it is a description of the transfer rather than an accusation.

cards.title: Cognitive Decentering
cards.prompt: What does decentering change without removing resistance?
cards.answer: It stops a momentary thought from automatically defining identity or available behaviour.

cards.title: Cognitive Decentering
cards.prompt: What is the practical sequence of cognitive decentering?
cards.answer: Notice the thought, label it as a mental event, question it, then choose an action.

cards.title: Comfortable Mediocrity Loop
cards.prompt: How can the comfortable mediocrity loop be interrupted without manufacturing a crisis?
cards.answer: Keep the discrepancy visible, remove one easy environmental exit, and convert it into one bounded action. Repetition supplies new identity evidence without requiring danger or deprivation.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: In what sense is perception a "controlled hallucination"?
cards.answer: The brain generates a predictive model of what should be happening and corrects it against sensory input. What is experienced is the model, so reality is inferred rather than seen directly.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What distinguishes perception from awareness, in this layering?
cards.answer: Awareness is registering input. Perception is the interpretation layer — the brain constructs meaning from partial signals rather than receiving raw data, so it is active reconstruction rather than passive reception.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What does mapping a neural correlate leave unexplained?
cards.answer: Qualia — the felt quality of the experience. You can specify the full mechanism for seeing red and still not have touched what it is like to see it.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What does panpsychism claim that physicalism does not?
cards.answer: That consciousness is fundamental to reality rather than emergent from complexity — all matter carries some proto-conscious property, and human consciousness is an elaborate instance of a universal one.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: Why is observer distance the functional basis of emotional regulation?
cards.answer: Because nothing can be regulated that has not first been observed. Fused with a thought there is only reaction; the gap between noticing it and acting on it is where any choice exists at all.

cards.title: Constraint Compression
cards.prompt: What is learned when a compressed deadline proves infeasible?
cards.answer: The exercise still identifies essential work, dependencies, and safety or quality constraints. Compression is an inspection tool, not a command to preserve an impossible date.

cards.title: Contextual Interference
cards.prompt: Why can worse performance during practice indicate better learning?
cards.answer: Variable, interleaved conditions remove the previous attempt’s momentum. The learner must select and reconstruct the response, producing errors that feedback can correct and a skill that is less tied to one prepared context.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What are the four motivations running most of what people say?
cards.answer: The need to impress, to be liked, to dominate, and to be understood. Everyone cycles through all four, but one usually hums underneath nearly everything a given person says.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What does banter demonstrate that depth alone cannot?
cards.answer: Presence, quickness and security at once — you caught what was said, did something with it, and can be challenged without being threatened. Depth creates intimacy but also weight; banter is the relief.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What is being felt as "chemistry" between two people?
cards.answer: Neural synchrony. With genuine presence, breathing, micro-expressions and energy align through mirror-neuron mirroring — the sensation is real and the mechanism is neurobiological rather than mystical.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Where does the laugh in genuine humour actually come from?
cards.answer: The accuracy of the observation, not the attempt at wit. Trying to be funny overrides the room; noticing something true and stating it precisely is what lands.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why are most conversations forgettable even when they go fine?
cards.answer: They are information exchanges, and the brain does not store those. What it retains is emotional state and moments of genuine connection — which covering ground does not produce.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why can a conversation drain you when nothing obviously went wrong?
cards.answer: A performative exchange costs cognitive effort and returns no reward, which produces a mild cortisol response. The brain is registering a losing trade and starting to look for the exit.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why does saying less often produce a better conversation?
cards.answer: Because the memorable part is the other person’s experience of being received. Space to think out loud and feel heard produces “that was a good talk” even when you contributed almost nothing.

cards.title: Deep Work
cards.prompt: How should an internal open loop be handled during a deep-work session?
cards.answer: Write it down in a trusted place and return to the task instead of solving it mid-session.

cards.title: Deep Work
cards.prompt: What distinguishes deep work from merely spending time at a desk?
cards.answer: One demanding task remains uninterrupted long enough for deeper connections to form.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: What distinguishes hard dopamine from easy dopamine, given they are chemically the same?
cards.answer: The effort-to-reward ratio and the delay. Easy dopamine is instant, costless and empty within minutes; hard dopamine is delayed, effortful, and compounds into something that raises the real-world reward gradient.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: What is the realistic timeline for baseline recovery, against the one-day version?
cards.answer: Days 3–7 for withdrawal to stabilise, weeks 2–4 before natural rewards register again, and one to three months for substantial receptor upregulation after heavy use.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why deliberately induce boredom before deep work?
cards.answer: To lower the baseline so the work itself becomes the reward source rather than competing with cheaper alternatives. Fifteen minutes of silence turns the session into relief instead of resistance.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why does quitting one cheap dopamine source so often produce a new one?
cards.answer: The drive is not switched off by removing a source — it redirects to the nearest available substitute. Quit pornography and the eating goes bad; quit games and the scrolling starts.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why is "dopamine detox" a category error?
cards.answer: There is nothing to flush. Dopamine is synthesised continuously and is central to motivation, movement and learning. What the protocol actually changes is the baseline, by letting downregulated receptors recover.

cards.title: Emotional Coherence
cards.prompt: What does emotional coherence protect when evidence threatens a belief?
cards.answer: It protects the identity, belonging, causal story, and meaning organized around the belief; dismissing the evidence can feel cheaper than rebuilding that model.

cards.title: Emotional Literacy
cards.prompt: Why should an emotion be treated as a hypothesis rather than a command?
cards.answer: It contains information about the person’s appraisal and state, but its first explanation may be incomplete or wrong. Naming, contextual checking, and delay preserve the information without surrendering the action to it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: What is "energy" in a social context, stated neurologically?
cards.answer: The aggregate signal of nervous system state — broadcast continuously through micro-expressions, vocal tone, movement quality and breathing rate, and picked up by other nervous systems through co-regulation.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why can't confidence be performed convincingly at close range?
cards.answer: The signals are too fine-grained and too involuntary. Performed confidence has a different acoustic, postural and micro-expression profile from the real thing, and other nervous systems register the mismatch without naming it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why can't presence be summoned mid-conversation by trying harder?
cards.answer: Because the attention was already divided in advance — by the phone in the pocket and the next appointment. Presence is set up before the interaction, not willed during it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why does ordinary undivided attention register as extraordinary?
cards.answer: Because almost nobody gives it. Most people in conversation are planning a reply, monitoring how they look and tracking other commitments at the same time — so full presence is rare enough to be felt as magnetic.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why is presence a prerequisite for reading people rather than a separate skill?
cards.answer: Because the data is subtle and fast — subtext under the words, the shift beneath a topic change, the micro-expression before the controlled response. Half-attention does not have the bandwidth to catch any of it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why is presence attunement rather than a fixed state?
cards.answer: Because it has to meet the specific person. Matching their energy — animated with excitement, still with seriousness — is what signals that you are actually tracking them rather than performing a constant.

cards.title: Environmental Context Collapse
cards.prompt: Why can one room serving every function make both work and rest harder?
cards.answer: The room has learned incompatible predictions. Entering it no longer supplies a clean cue for either state, so attention must resolve the conflict deliberately.

cards.title: Environmental Design
cards.prompt: What is the central environmental-design move?
cards.answer: Make the desired behavior easy and visible, while making its competitor hard and hidden, so the recurring context rehearses the choice before willpower is needed.

cards.title: Exercise–Learning Coupling
cards.prompt: What two different jobs does exercise–learning coupling assign to movement and novelty?
cards.answer: Exercise supports the biological supply environment; novel learning recruits and repeatedly uses cells in active circuits. Neither job is identical to the other.

cards.title: Familiarity-Understanding Gap
cards.prompt: What closes the familiarity-understanding gap?
cards.answer: Effortful recall, explanation and application that test whether the idea can actually be used.

cards.title: Familiarity-Understanding Gap
cards.prompt: What creates the familiarity-understanding gap?
cards.answer: Repeated exposure feels fluent, and that fluency is mistaken for retrievable or usable knowledge.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What does the prisoner's dilemma actually demonstrate?
cards.answer: That individually rational choices can produce a collectively worse outcome. Betrayal is better whatever the other does, so both betray and both land on five years where mutual silence would have cost one.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What four properties made tit-for-tat win Axelrod's tournament?
cards.answer: It is cooperative, retaliatory, forgiving and transparent — it invites good outcomes, cannot be exploited, escapes mutual-defection loops, and is legible enough that partners learn what to expect.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What is the arbitrage in recognising a positive-sum game before the other party does?
cards.answer: Terms that look generous under zero-sum logic are merely ordinary under positive-sum logic. The person who sees the frame correctly can offer them and capture disproportionate value.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why can a Nash equilibrium be stable and bad at the same time?
cards.answer: Because stability only means no one gains by moving alone. Everyone can be worse off than an alternative arrangement and still be unable to reach it without coordinated movement.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why is dominance fast to establish and fragile to hold?
cards.answer: It compels compliance rather than attracting it, which generates resentment and provokes coalitional resistance. It has to be continuously re-imposed, where prestige accumulates goodwill instead.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why treat almost every interaction as a repeated game?
cards.answer: Because most are, and the asymmetry is stark: the cost of generosity in a genuinely one-shot game is trivial, while an aggressive win becomes expensive the moment the game turns out to be repeated.

cards.title: Health Signaling Theory
cards.prompt: Why can no single feature compensate for poor systemic health, on this theory?
cards.answer: Because the signals are integrated holistically. Symmetry, skin, body composition and secondary sexual characteristics are read together as one inference about genetic quality and vitality, so a deficit shows across the set.

cards.title: Hormone Optimization
cards.prompt: Why is stress management a hormonal intervention rather than a soft one?
cards.answer: Because chronic Cortisol lowers testosterone directly. Stress is not adjacent to the endocrine system here — it is one of the suppression pathways acting on it, alongside plastics and processed food.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: What makes lucid dreaming neurologically unusual?
cards.answer: It combines two things that normally exclude each other — metacognition, which waking has without immersion, and full dream simulation, which dreaming has without metacognition.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why does reality testing use text specifically?
cards.answer: Because text is unstable in dreams — it changes when you look away and back. The waking habit has to run for weeks before it transfers into a dream, where the instability becomes the giveaway.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why is rehearsal inside a lucid dream higher fidelity than waking visualisation?
cards.answer: Waking mental imagery fires motor circuits at roughly 30–40% of actual movement; during REM the same imagery fires them at close to 100%.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why is Wake-Back-To-Bed the most reliable lucidity technique?
cards.answer: Returning to sleep after five or six hours re-enters REM directly and extends it. Lucid dreams occur almost exclusively in REM, and REM loads the second half of the night.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: How does gaslighting manufacture its own evidence?
cards.answer: The sustained stress it creates raises cortisol, which degrades hippocampal memory reliability. The gaslighter then points at the unreliable memory as proof the target cannot trust their own perception.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What makes an identity lever like "smart people know that…" work without an argument?
cards.answer: It does not assert a claim; it defines what the listener’s self-concept requires. Agreeing is then the only move that keeps them consistent with who they take themselves to be.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does "this closes tomorrow" outperform "sign up now"?
cards.answer: Loss aversion is asymmetric — losing feels worse than an equivalent gain feels good. Framing the offer as a loss to be avoided pulls harder than framing the same offer as a gain to be taken.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does a story slip past the resistance a fact provokes?
cards.answer: A story can recruit simulation and identification, reducing active counter-argument while attention is inside it. That makes narrative persuasive, not immune to later scrutiny.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does alternating warmth and cruelty bind harder than steady warmth?
cards.answer: Unpredictable reward drives more dopamine than consistent reward, and contrast makes the good moments read as better than they are. The resulting pattern is indistinguishable from substance addiction, so leaving is withdrawal.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does offering a small payment make a request less likely to be granted?
cards.answer: It converts a social exchange into a market one. Once the transaction is priced, the small sum is judged against market rates and reads as insulting — where reciprocity had been carrying it.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why leave the moral of a persuasive story unstated?
cards.answer: Because a conclusion the listener draws themselves registers as their own idea, and people commit far harder to ideas they believe they generated than to ones handed to them.

cards.title: Manufactured Division
cards.prompt: What is the bounded form of manufactured division?
cards.answer: A grievance is routed through identity, extreme opponents receive disproportionate attention, and conflict displaces inquiry into shared causes. This can emerge from aligned incentives without proving one hidden controller.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What do focused attention and open monitoring each train?
cards.answer: Focused attention trains the prefrontal-parietal control network — sustaining and returning attention to one object. Open monitoring trains metacognitive awareness: observing the stream without fixing on any part of it.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What does quieting the default mode network change outside of meditation itself?
cards.answer: The resting state. The DMN generates mind-wandering, rumination and the constant internal narrative, and practice quiets it during rest as well as during sitting.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What is meditation actually training, if not relaxation?
cards.answer: Attention. The practice is noticing that attention has moved and returning it — repeatedly, for a set duration. The returning is the exercise, not the stillness.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why are meditation and the attention economy antagonistic rather than complementary?
cards.answer: They condition opposite programs on the same hardware — one trains hyperreactivity to novelty and compulsive checking, the other sustained focus and tolerance for boredom. What decides it is which gets more repetitions.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why does labelling an experience reduce its intensity?
cards.answer: The labelling activates the prefrontal cortex and dampens the amygdala response. Naming an emotion is itself a regulating act, not merely a description of one.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why is reduced amygdala reactivity in meditators not emotional suppression?
cards.answer: Because the response is recalibrated rather than blocked. The system is answering to actual threat instead of predicted threat, so the spike is smaller and briefer rather than stifled.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: If melatonin is not a sedative, what does it actually do?
cards.answer: It signals darkness. Its presence lowers core temperature, shifts the autonomic system toward parasympathetic dominance and suppresses cortisol — creating the conditions under which sleep can begin, rather than causing it.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: What are the two biologically distinct melatonins?
cards.answer: Pineal melatonin, secreted into the bloodstream as the body’s darkness signal, and intracellular melatonin, produced inside mitochondria in response to infrared light. The second never enters the blood and acts locally as an antioxidant.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why does supplementation have more evidential support in older adults?
cards.answer: Because the deficit is real there. The pineal gland calcifies with age and natural production genuinely declines, where in a younger person late melatonin is usually a behavioural timing problem instead.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why is the "teenage night owl" biological rather than behavioural?
cards.answer: Puberty shifts melatonin onset about two hours later. The adolescent is not physiologically ready for sleep at the adult time, which is why school start times before 8:30 AM run against the biology.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why might a supraphysiological melatonin dose make things worse over time?
cards.answer: It can desensitise melatonin receptors and suppress the body’s own production through negative feedback — so the supplement gradually creates the deficit it was taken to correct.

cards.title: Mental Rehearsal
cards.prompt: What boundary separates mental rehearsal from performance fantasy?
cards.answer: Rehearsal targets a specific real action and feeds into execution and feedback. Fantasy ends at the imagined outcome and therefore cannot correct the model against the environment.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: How does an abundance of options damage satisfaction with any one of them?
cards.answer: It installs a permanently elevated reference point. Knowing hundreds of alternatives exist means every real person is measured against an idealised projection, so the shortfall is architectural rather than about them.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What happens when the attachment system is activated and then repeatedly frustrated?
cards.answer: It adapts by suppressing the activation. Intimacy cues stop being treated as worth investing in, because the investment has repeatedly gone unreciprocated at the attachment level.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What have dating apps successfully substituted for the goal users came with?
cards.answer: The process itself. Swiping, matching and the validation become the reward, which keeps people on the app — and the app benefits precisely from the connection not being reached.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What is limerence for, if it is not love?
cards.answer: It is a recruitment drive — a neurochemical state producing enough obsession to sustain the start of pair-bonding. It has a shelf life of roughly 6–18 months, and what was built underneath it is what remains.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: Why is eager availability a weak signal in evolutionary terms?
cards.answer: In the ancestral environment it could indicate low status or an absence of other options. Engaged unavailability signals that other demands compete for the person’s time, which reads as status.

cards.title: Money as a Coordination Claim
cards.prompt: What gives a currency token purchasing power on this account?
cards.answer: Social and institutional acceptance in exchange and settlement, not its physical material.

cards.title: Money as a Coordination Claim
cards.prompt: Why does commodity backing not eliminate the coordination problem?
cards.answer: Convertibility still depends on an issuer, reserve rules and a legal settlement system.

cards.title: Motivation-to-Automaticity Bridge
cards.prompt: What role does motivation play in the motivation-to-automaticity bridge?
cards.answer: Temporary scaffolding that starts repetitions during the expensive early phase.

cards.title: Motivation-to-Automaticity Bridge
cards.prompt: Why should intense emotional motivation have an exit condition?
cards.answer: Otherwise continuing requires repeatedly reopening the original wound instead of converting drive into structure.

cards.title: Music as State Regulation
cards.prompt: What makes music a state-regulation tool rather than a magical treatment?
cards.answer: Its combined effects on prediction, motor anticipation, arousal, attention, and learned association can shape what the listener does next; no special tuning frequency is required.

cards.title: Norm Calibration
cards.prompt: How does a standard differ from a goal in norm calibration?
cards.answer: A goal is a distant outcome; a standard is the floor that current behaviour is expected to meet. Calibration changes when the supporting action becomes ordinary, not when the outcome is merely declared normal.

cards.title: Novelty-Cadence Conditioning
cards.prompt: How is novelty-cadence conditioning retrained?
cards.answer: By gradually extending uninterrupted time with one context before switching.

cards.title: Novelty-Cadence Conditioning
cards.prompt: What response does a rapid novelty feed rehearse when discomfort appears?
cards.answer: Switching immediately to a new stimulus rather than elaborating the current one.

cards.title: Novelty Substitution
cards.prompt: What evidence is missing when novelty is substituted for compatibility?
cards.answer: Behaviour across stress, conflict, routine, care, and repair. Novel intensity reports a state; it does not provide the longitudinal pattern needed to compare relationships.

cards.title: Pattern Over Tells
cards.prompt: What evidence must exist before a behavioral tell supports an inference?
cards.answer: An individual baseline, a deviation, recurrence in comparable contexts, and an audit of plausible alternatives and the observer’s own bias.

cards.title: Pattern Recognition
cards.prompt: What decides whether a pattern match stays automatic or reaches conscious attention?
cards.answer: Routine matches stay automatic; novel or complex cases rise into conscious processing.

cards.title: Pattern Recognition
cards.prompt: Why is a bodily intuition signal not proof that a prediction is correct?
cards.answer: It shows that below-awareness processing produced a conclusion, not that the underlying pattern library was accurate.

cards.title: Perceptual Gating
cards.prompt: What is the difference between perceptual gating and creating reality?
cards.answer: Gating changes which available signals enter the conscious model and how they are interpreted. It does not create external facts; prediction error can still show that the model was wrong.

cards.title: Posture and Movement
cards.prompt: What makes posture the first move among the health signals?
cards.answer: Its cost. Every other signal takes money or time; posture can be corrected immediately at no expense, which puts it ahead of the interventions that need either.

cards.title: Process-Reward Association
cards.prompt: What do stable ritual cues contribute to a process-reward association?
cards.answer: They reduce initiation decisions and make the start of work more predictable.

cards.title: Process-Reward Association
cards.prompt: Why is process-reward association retained as a behavioural claim?
cards.answer: The source invokes dopamine and myelination but supplies no biological measurement.

cards.title: Relationship Medium Substitution
cards.prompt: What is substituted in relationship medium substitution?
cards.answer: An easily observed platform signal substitutes for harder evidence about the relationship. Contact can express care, but its frequency is not identical to intimacy and its absence is not identical to rejection.

cards.title: Response Within Constraint
cards.prompt: How does response within constraint differ from resignation?
cards.answer: It accepts only the part that cannot be changed now, then directs agency toward stance and remaining action. Resignation treats the whole field as fixed.

cards.title: Retaliation Escalation Loop
cards.prompt: What shared assumption does “an eye for an eye” require to produce closure?
cards.answer: Both parties must agree on the original harm, the proportional response and when the balance is settled.

cards.title: Retaliation Escalation Loop
cards.prompt: Why does retaliation tend to escalate when that accounting is disputed?
cards.answer: The recipient experiences payback as a new injury and treats it as justification for another response.

cards.title: Scheduled Commitment
cards.prompt: What decision does a scheduled commitment remove from execution time?
cards.answer: Whether the current mood grants permission to begin. The priority, time, and first action were chosen earlier; execution starts from the cue rather than reopening the goal debate.

cards.title: Seiri (Sort) – Part of the 5S System
cards.prompt: In what sense is decluttering a cognitive intervention rather than an aesthetic one?
cards.answer: The visual cortex processes disorder continuously, drawing on the same resources focus and creativity need. Removing objects buys attention back; the tidiness is a side effect.

cards.title: Seiton (Set in Order) – Part of the 5S System
cards.prompt: Why must seiri precede seiton?
cards.answer: Because arranging what should have been discarded only produces a well-labelled surplus. Sorting decides what exists; setting in order removes the search cost for what survived.

cards.title: Self-Respect Through Kept Promises
cards.prompt: Why does action come before the feeling in this model of self-respect?
cards.answer: Self-trust is inferred from evidence. Repeatedly keeping a bounded promise supplies evidence that one’s commitments matter; waiting to feel worthy withholds the behavior that could produce it.

cards.title: Skin Health
cards.prompt: Why does the source prioritise internal optimisation over topical products for skin?
cards.answer: Because skin is a readout, not the system. It sits downstream of gut, sleep and endocrine state, so a topical product treats the display while whatever is generating it continues unchanged.

cards.title: State Cross-Validation
cards.prompt: Why is an idea stronger after state cross-validation?
cards.answer: It has survived both the state that makes possibilities visible and the state that exposes logistical constraints. Endorsement by only one state leaves the other’s information unused.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What does a credential actually signal, beyond its content?
cards.answer: That you are the kind of person who got through that selection process — conscientiousness and intelligence. It is a costly signal, and the knowledge is close to a side effect.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What does uptalk signal, and what is the alternative failure mode?
cards.answer: Uptalk — pitch rising at the end of a statement — signals approval-seeking, turning assertions into questions. Monotone fails the other way and signals disengagement; confident speech varies without pleading.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What is the clearest single status signal, and why does it work?
cards.answer: Comfort in silence. Rushing to fill a gap treats the gap as a failure to be entertaining; tolerating it signals that your value does not depend on this interaction going well.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why can't nonchalance be performed successfully over time?
cards.answer: Performing it requires continuously suppressing the real responses, and the effort of the suppression leaks into the signals. Others’ nervous systems register that something is being held down even when they cannot name it.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why does willingness to disagree make your agreement worth more?
cards.answer: Because agreement inflation has made assent nearly free. Someone who will say “I see it differently” makes their “yes” carry information, which is why calm disagreement increases rather than reduces attention.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why is the informal energy hierarchy in a room often not the official one?
cards.answer: Because the pull goes to whoever is most present, most regulated and least concerned with impressing anyone — which is a different quality from holding the title.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why is the status response automatic rather than a judgement you make?
cards.answer: It runs on an ancient, fast system that evolved when group standing was a survival variable. Listening harder and laughing more readily at a high-status person happens before any conscious decision about them.

cards.title: Stimulus–Response Gap
cards.prompt: What does the stimulus–response gap change without suppressing emotion?
cards.answer: It changes whether the first emotion automatically becomes the public act. The feeling remains input; pausing allows it to be named, contextualised, and answered proportionately.

cards.title: Strategic Adaptation
cards.prompt: What prevents action bias from turning strategic adaptation into escalation?
cards.answer: A stopping rule. Fast execution must be paired with explicit conditions for consolidation, defense, pause, or exit; otherwise the original advantage becomes the reason not to stop.

cards.title: Strategic Understatement
cards.prompt: How can understatement produce more information?
cards.answer: Withholding correction or asking for explanation lets the other person reveal assumptions and reasoning.

cards.title: Strategic Understatement
cards.prompt: What distinction makes strategic understatement possible?
cards.answer: Possessing knowledge or emotion is separate from displaying all of it.

cards.title: Synaptic Construction
cards.prompt: Why should synaptic construction be separated from myelination?
cards.answer: Establishing and strengthening communication is the foundation; myelination changes transmission efficiency along existing axons. A difficult new response cannot be explained only as an uninsulated finished route.

cards.title: Task–Emotion Mapping
cards.prompt: Why is “use more discipline” a poor generic response to procrastination?
cards.answer: Perfectionism, overwhelm, boredom, outcome anxiety, and genuine misalignment are different predicted costs. One force-based response leaves those distinctions—and therefore the relevant intervention—unknown.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: What was Edison's ball-bearing trick actually detecting?
cards.answer: The border of sleep. Holding the bearings meant that dropping them signalled he had crossed out of hypnagogia into sleep — letting him work the theta window without losing it.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why do good ideas arrive in the shower rather than at the desk?
cards.answer: Prefrontal executive control normally directs association toward expected connections. In low-constraint, theta-adjacent states that constraint loosens and associative cortices link across far wider domains.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why do parental messages become identity architecture rather than opinions?
cards.answer: They arrive while the child is predominantly in theta and alpha, where the critical filter is not yet operating. Nothing evaluates them, so they are absorbed as structure rather than as claims.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why does trying harder collapse a theta practice?
cards.answer: Effort activates beta, and beta closes the window. The state is held by loose, low-effort awareness — the instruction is to observe and suggest rather than to push.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: How does the kintsugi framing avoid becoming toxic positivity?
cards.answer: It makes no claim that the damage was good. It claims only that the repair can be visible and honoured, and that the repaired self carries a history the unbroken one does not.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What does a narrow window of tolerance mean in practice?
cards.answer: That inputs a regulated system would process neutrally — a raised voice, an unexpected touch — trigger full threat responses, because the system is calibrated to a historical threat level rather than a present one.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What is collective or cumulative trauma, as distinct from acute trauma?
cards.answer: ixcarus groups chronic emotional absence, economic stress, inherited scarcity, and isolation as cumulative adversity that may shape regulation. That grouping does not by itself establish trauma or rule PTSD in or out.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What is titration, and why not simply avoid or flood?
cards.answer: Gradual exposure at a manageable dose. The window of tolerance widens through successful approach — avoidance never tests it, and flooding overwhelms it, so neither expands anything.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: Where does trauma actually reside, if not in the event?
cards.answer: In the sources’ model, an overwhelming response was not integrated, so later cues can reactivate defensive expectations. This is one account of trauma’s persistence, not its complete clinical definition.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: Why doesn't knowing where a trauma pattern came from deactivate it?
cards.answer: Because the survival program runs before conscious awareness engages. Insight arrives after the nervous system has already acted, so understanding the origin leaves the physiological program intact.

cards.title: Unstimulated Incubation
cards.prompt: What makes an interval incubation rather than merely downtime?
cards.answer: A prior problem or experience is allowed to remain active while no new high-demand media stream replaces it. Low-demand movement can remain; externally selected input is what is withheld.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: By this definition, is the house you live in an asset?
cards.answer: In ixcarus’s cash-flow heuristic, an owner-occupied house consumes cash while a rental can produce it. In accounting terms, a residence may still be an asset; the heuristic asks about cash direction rather than replacing the formal category.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: What does leverage actually mean here?
cards.answer: Effort deployed once that keeps paying — code, content and capital all scale without further hours. A job pays once per hour worked; a deployed asset pays indefinitely on a fixed investment.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why does starting early beat starting big?
cards.answer: Starting earlier gives returns more periods to compound. It does not guarantee that any small early sum beats any larger later sum; return, duration, fees, and contributions determine the comparison.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why does the brain prefer certain mediocrity to uncertain improvement?
cards.answer: In the source’s model, a certain present income feels safer than an uncertain possible improvement. That preference may reflect loss aversion, but the decision must also account for the venture’s real probability and cost of failure.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why is linear income structurally capped regardless of the rate?
cards.answer: It is bounded by a finite, non-renewable input — perhaps ten sustainable working hours a day. A higher hourly rate raises the ceiling without removing it.

cards.title: Adult Neurogenesis
cards.prompt: Why are birth and functional integration different claims in adult neurogenesis?
cards.answer: A new cell can fail to survive or join an active circuit. The source treats production as raw supply and challenging use as part of the process that recruits and retains it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: What changes once a political opinion is held as identity?
cards.answer: A challenge to it stops being a disagreement and becomes an existential threat, which is what licenses dehumanising the person making it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: Which pre-existing feature of attention does the engagement loop exploit?
cards.answer: Negativity bias. Threatening and enraging material already commands disproportionate attention, so an algorithm measuring attention finds anger and keeps supplying it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: Why does optimising for engagement radicalise a user base rather than merely entertain it?
cards.answer: If outrage earns more time and reactions, an engagement objective can select more of it. That can create a radicalizing feedback path, although the metric does not force every feed or user to reach that endpoint.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: How does convenience produce an inability to motivate oneself?
cards.answer: By removing the resistance the aMCC trains on. Eliminating friction at every point leaves the structure unused, and unused capacity degrades — so the deficit is atrophy, not character.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: What distinguishes embodied discipline from forced discipline?
cards.answer: What is being changed. Forced discipline white-knuckles the same brain structure and regresses when willpower runs out; embodied discipline builds the structure, so the same behaviour costs less each year.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: What is the training stimulus for aMCC growth?
cards.answer: Resistance — the experience of “I don’t want to do this” followed by doing it anyway. The stimulus is the override itself, not the difficulty or the suffering.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why does athletic training appear to make people more disciplined outside the gym?
cards.answer: Because the structure it builds is not sport-specific. A larger aMCC transfers to emotional regulation, cognitive persistence and social courage — the “general discipline” is shared infrastructure.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why does the type of resistance not matter for aMCC growth?
cards.answer: Because the signal it responds to is overriding the preference for comfort, not the domain the override happens in. A hard conversation and a workout supply the same stimulus.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why start a resistance protocol with small resistances rather than large ones?
cards.answer: Because the active ingredient is the completed override, and it accrues by reps. A resistance too large to finish supplies no signal — the aMCC responds to progressive overload, like muscle.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What is dorsal vagal shutdown protecting against, and when did it evolve to fire?
cards.answer: Overwhelming, inescapable threat — the state that follows once fight and flight have both failed. Under chronic unresolvable stress it presents as apathy, which is protection rather than laziness.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What is the characteristic experience of anhedonia?
cards.answer: Remembering that you liked something while being unable to feel why. The memory of the reward survives; the reward response does not.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What test distinguishes contentment from managed numbness?
cards.answer: Twenty minutes without stimulation. Genuine calm tolerates stillness; a depleted baseline produces automatic phone reaches and restlessness — the quiet of absence rather than peace.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why can emotional flatness not distinguish apathy from depression by itself?
cards.answer: Apathy names reduced motivation and anhedonia reduced pleasure, while depression can include both. The dimensions overlap rather than forming opposite diagnoses.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does a working reward system stop registering genuinely good events?
cards.answer: Because it recalibrated rather than broke. Chronic artificial spikes raise the threshold for feeling anything, and ordinary life cannot compete with what the baseline was set against.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does cutting artificial stimulation make things worse before better?
cards.answer: The spikes were the only input clearing the raised threshold. Removing them leaves nothing registering until the baseline itself falls, so the grey deepens before colour returns.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does the recovery protocol put physical inputs before cognitive ones?
cards.answer: Because the nervous system responds to movement, sunlight and cold before it responds to reasoning. Getting the body out of dorsal vagal has to come first — cognition applied to a shut-down system does not land.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: What actually blocks most people from financial independence, if not a low income?
cards.answer: The gap between earned and consumed. Assets can only accumulate out of that difference, so a large income spent entirely builds nothing.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: What structural property caps labour income no matter how well paid it is?
cards.answer: It is sold in hours, and hours are finite. Raising the rate raises the ceiling but does not remove it, and the income stops the moment you do.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: Which property of asset income does labour income lack entirely?
cards.answer: Compounding. Asset income can be reinvested to produce more income; an hour worked produces its wage once and nothing after.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: Why does a good salary make the job trap harder to leave rather than easier?
cards.answer: Because it makes the trap comfortable. High labour income raises the standard of living the exit would have to be funded past, so the better the wage the more the handcuffs are worth.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: What can disclosure change about a physical signal?
cards.answer: Its interpretation. Context can make the same trait look like a byproduct of broader capability or a goal in itself, but disclosure does not change the body or prove that either reading is accurate.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: What is the error in optimising the aesthetic feature directly?
cards.answer: It targets the proxy rather than what the proxy indicates. The detection system is reading health; a surgically produced jawline supplies the shape without the underlying signals it was standing for.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why does facial symmetry register as attractive?
cards.answer: It signals developmental stability. Parasites and stress during development produce asymmetry, so symmetry is evidence of a body that grew without those insults.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is posture unusual among the attraction levers?
cards.answer: It changes the hormones as well as the signal, and it costs nothing. Upright open posture raises testosterone and lowers cortisol — so correcting it improves the underlying state, not only the appearance of it.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is sleep the highest-impact lever on physical attractiveness?
cards.answer: Because so many separate signals run through it. Skin quality, eye quality, cortisol and therefore testosterone, and hormonal regulation are all downstream of sleep — one input moving several read-outs at once.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: What premise does the blackpill share with the looksmaxxing community?
cards.answer: That attraction scores fixed individual morphology — bone structure, ratios, angles. They differ only in the conclusion drawn: futility on one side, surgery on the other.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: Why does fixed bone structure not make self-improvement futile?
cards.answer: Because the fixed part is one input among many. The signals attraction reads are spread across dozens of features, and most of them — body composition, hormones, skin quality, posture, movement — respond to effort.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: Why does improving several health signals beat perfecting one feature?
cards.answer: The assessment compounds across signals instead of scoring the strongest. Average features on a genuinely healthy body outrank strong features with poor health behind them.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Cortisol supports testosterone in the morning but suppresses it chronically. What does that distinction turn on?
cards.answer: Acute versus sustained elevation. A short morning surge is supportive; keeping cortisol up through the day — which late caffeine does — flips the effect.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: What does early morning light do that makes it high leverage at zero cost?
cards.answer: Two things at once: it anchors the circadian rhythm and triggers the cortisol awakening response. One free input sets both the day’s timing and its alertness.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Why are eight hours at a random time not equivalent to eight hours at a fixed one?
cards.answer: The circadian system responds to consistency, not duration alone. Irregular timing disrupts cortisol timing, sleep architecture and the alertness window even when the total is adequate.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Why delay caffeine roughly two hours after waking?
cards.answer: Because the cortisol awakening response is already supplying alertness. Caffeine taken into it compounds rather than complements, and the larger combined peak makes the later crash worse.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What does Alexander having no answer to "what comes after conquering everything" expose?
cards.answer: That the goal was never terminal. A project justified by proving you are the greatest has no completion condition, so finishing it leaves nothing behind it.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What does Diogenes throwing away his cup demonstrate?
cards.answer: That a possession can be revealed as unnecessary by a single counterexample. The cup had seemed like a minimum; a child drinking from cupped hands showed it was baggage.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What is the modern Cynic critique, stated without the jar?
cards.answer: That the objects being worked for mostly exist to be seen by other people. Forty years are traded for a house rarely occupied and a car whose function is to signal to strangers.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: Where does Cynicism locate freedom?
cards.answer: In wanting less, not in acquiring more. The route to it is subtraction of artificial convention rather than accumulation against it.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: Why would the most powerful man alive envy a man who owned nothing?
cards.answer: Because Diogenes already had what the conquest was for. Alexander was chasing freedom through acquisition and remained bound to being seen as great; Diogenes had reached it by needing nothing.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What is the most reliable detection signal, given that the behaviour itself may look fine?
cards.answer: Your own state. Feeling consistently confused, diminished or off-balance around someone — and clearer and more capable away from them — is data the constructed mask cannot suppress.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What is the primary protection against dark triad dynamics?
cards.answer: Walk-away power. The leverage comes from your dependence on the relationship, so having a real alternative is worth more than detecting any individual tactic.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What makes gaslighting self-reinforcing at the neurological level?
cards.answer: The stress it creates degrades hippocampal memory reliability via cortisol. The resulting confusion is then presented as proof that your perception was the problem all along.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What separates Machiavellianism from narcissism in what drives the behaviour?
cards.answer: Narcissism is driven by emotional need — a fragile self-image requiring propping up. Machiavellianism is driven by strategic advantage, with people treated as instruments rather than as validators.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: Why do dark triad profiles come across as unusually charming at first?
cards.answer: Fewer internal inhibitions read as confidence, and the mask has been deliberately constructed for impact. What looks like natural ease is the absence of the hesitation most people have.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: Why is a Machiavellian the hardest of the three to detect at work?
cards.answer: Because the behaviour is genuinely rational and cooperative right up until cooperation stops serving the goal. There is no emotional volatility to notice in advance.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What distinguishes projection from ordinary dislike?
cards.answer: The intensity. Mild dislike is preference; disproportionate, specific rage is recognition — the trait is being seen rather than merely disliked.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What does a defence mechanism do to a conflict?
cards.answer: Moves it out of sight, not out of existence. The conflict keeps running below consciousness — what changes is your access to it, not its activity.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What is the ordering that makes rationalisation a defence rather than reasoning?
cards.answer: The decision came first and the logic after. The explanation is manufactured to cover an emotional outcome already reached, which is why it always arrives fully formed and always favours the same conclusion.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why is repression more dangerous than a memory you can still reach?
cards.answer: Because it keeps its influence while losing its address. The buried moment still decides how you flinch and still runs the relationships, but there is no longer anything conscious to trace the behaviour back to.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why is the serial cheater convinced his partner is cheating?
cards.answer: He is projecting his own model outward. He knows how easy it is, so he assumes everyone runs the same game — describing himself while pointing at her.

cards.title: Derealization
cards.prompt: How does the source distinguish derealization from ordinary distraction?
cards.answer: Attention is not merely elsewhere; the whole scene loses felt immediacy, as though information is being processed across a membrane rather than inhabited as experience.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: What is receptor downregulation, and what triggers it?
cards.answer: The brain cutting receptor count and sensitivity to compensate for chronic overstimulation. It is a protective adjustment to too much signal, and it is what drops the baseline.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: What is the goal of recalibration, if not zero stimulation?
cards.answer: A narrower spike range. The baseline can only stabilise if the peaks stop overshooting it — variance, not abstinence, is the target.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why does swapping social media for Netflix change nothing?
cards.answer: The baseline responds to spike magnitude, not to the source. Substituting one high-intensity input for another keeps the threshold exactly where it was.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why does the baseline drop further in the first days of recalibration?
cards.answer: The downregulated receptors are still downregulated while the input that was compensating for them is gone. Recovery of sensitivity lags the removal of the spikes, which is why days 2–5 are the hardest.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why is "dopamine detox" the wrong name for the process?
cards.answer: Dopamine cannot be eliminated — it is not a toxin to clear. What is being restored is baseline sensitivity, by narrowing the spike range rather than removing the neurotransmitter.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What counts as "cost" in the brain's pricing of a task?
cards.answer: Uncertainty, fear of failure, social judgment, ambiguity, cognitive effort and emotional discomfort — not only physical exertion. That is why two physically identical tasks can price completely differently.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What happens to motivation when perceived cost exceeds expected reward?
cards.answer: It disappears rather than diminishing. The calculation is not a dial that turns down — losing it flips the task to not worth starting, which is why willing yourself into it does not work.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What is the operational question to ask about a task you keep failing to start?
cards.answer: How many decisions stand between you and beginning. “Put shoes on and go” hides finding clothes, charging headphones, choosing a playlist, deciding the workout — each one a real cost.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: Why can one email feel impossible while forty-five minutes of scrolling is effortless?
cards.answer: Identical physical demand, opposite prices. The scroll carries no uncertainty or judgment; the email carries both, and the brain prices what you do not consciously see.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: Why do high performers wear identical clothes and keep fixed routines?
cards.answer: To remove decisions from the path, not to display discipline. If the friction is low enough the decision never has to be made, so motivation never has to cover it.

cards.title: Endocrine Disruptors
cards.prompt: Why are the page’s exposure-reduction suggestions not a treatment protocol?
cards.answer: The cited sources do not establish population effects or treatment outcomes for those recommendations.

cards.title: Endocrine Disruptors
cards.prompt: Why is “the body cannot tell the difference” too crude for endocrine disruptors?
cards.answer: A compound may activate, block or alter feedback differently by tissue and dose.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: If DNA is the music, what is the epigenome?
cards.answer: The reader deciding which songs play in which cell. Every cell holds the same score; the epigenome is what makes a liver cell play liver music and a neuron play neuron music.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: On Sinclair's model, what is ageing fundamentally?
cards.answer: A loss of information, not wear on parts. The instructions for which genes play in which cell degrade like a photocopy of a photocopy, and cells begin losing their identity.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: What goes wrong in a cell when the epigenetic reader is scratched?
cards.answer: Genes that should stay silent switch on and genes that should be playing shut off. The cell starts behaving like something other than what it is.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: Why is "your DNA is not your fate" a claim about leverage rather than optimism?
cards.answer: Because roughly 80% of future health and longevity sits in the epigenetic layer rather than the genes. The sequence is fixed; the reader is influenceable daily, so almost all the movable weight is on the modifiable side.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: How does chronic stress worsen estrogen dominance?
cards.answer: By suppressing progesterone, the hormone that balances estrogen in the luteal phase. Chemical exposure raises the estrogen signal from one side while cortisol removes the counterweight from the other.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Which organ governs estrogen clearance, and why does that make it a lever?
cards.answer: The liver. When it is overloaded, clearance slows and the signal accumulates — so supporting its metabolism, via indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables, acts on the exit rather than the entrance.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why can estrogen dominance occur without elevated estrogen?
cards.answer: Because receptors are finite and xenoestrogens compete for them. What is dominant is the estrogen-like signalling, which a blood concentration of real estrogen does not capture.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why can excessive high-intensity cardio work against hormonal balance?
cards.answer: It spikes cortisol enough to suppress reproductive hormones. The exercise is not the problem; the cortisol load from too much of the high-intensity kind is, which is why moderate volume is prescribed.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why does cutting dietary fat too far undermine sex hormone production?
cards.answer: Estrogen and progesterone are built from cholesterol. Below roughly 25–30% of calories from fat, the raw material for synthesis is missing.

cards.title: Eternal Recurrence
cards.prompt: What does an affirmative answer to the recurrence test not require?
cards.answer: Liking every event or endorsing every harm.

cards.title: Eternal Recurrence
cards.prompt: What is eternal recurrence used as on this page?
cards.answer: A diagnostic test of present choices, not a literal prediction about the universe.

cards.title: Fasting & Cognitive Performance
cards.prompt: What does feeling mentally clear during a fast fail to verify?
cards.answer: Ketosis, autophagy, immune repair or superior objective performance.

cards.title: Fasting & Cognitive Performance
cards.prompt: Why can the fasting source’s hour-by-hour timeline not be treated as universal?
cards.answer: It supplies no measurements, while diet, activity, health, medication and metabolism can shift the state.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: How does the thermostat enforce itself through spending?
cards.answer: By consuming money before it can be invested. Spending down to the familiar range keeps the balance inside the comfort zone without any conscious decision to stay poor.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Which part of the childhood money memory is the error, on this account?
cards.answer: Not the memory or the feeling — both were real. The error is the generalisation drawn from it: that money above a particular level means danger.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why can the financial ceiling not be argued away?
cards.answer: Because the amygdala updates on evidence, not reasoning. Exposure and survived actions are what change the threat tag; understanding the mechanism intellectually leaves the alarm exactly where it was.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does "the whole thing is rigged" get read as a fear response rather than a position?
cards.answer: Because it makes inaction feel like a political stance. The conclusion happens to license exactly the behaviour the ceiling requires, which is what marks it as a rationalisation.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does earning above the ceiling feel physically threatening?
cards.answer: Money is processed through the amygdala rather than the prefrontal cortex. Considering income above the setpoint fires the same alarm as physical danger, so the body treats the opportunity as a threat.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does the diagnostic depend on the first number rather than a considered one?
cards.answer: Because the ceiling is subconscious. Anything after the first reflex has been through rationalisation or aspirational inflation, both of which edit the belief you were trying to read.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: What does imaging show happening to the brain during dreaming?
cards.answer: Two opposite moves at once — the prefrontal region handling reasoning, reality-checking and suppression powers down, while the emotional core becomes more active than when awake.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: What is the difference between the questions Freud and Jung put to a dream?
cards.answer: Jung asked who you are beneath the mask; Freud asked what is hidden under it and why you put it there. One reads dreams as revelation of a self, the other as concealment of a wish.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Which dreams are worth attending to, on Freud's account?
cards.answer: The ones that land hard — waking you with your heart going, or staying with you all day. Emotional charge is the signal that something was sent up rather than merely generated.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Why are dreams incoherent, if their meaning is real?
cards.answer: The editor is offline. Morphing faces and impossible places are what raw emotion looks like without the machinery that normally makes experience coherent — the packaging is a mess, not the content.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Why does a wish have to appear in a dream disguised?
cards.answer: Because the dream is a compromise. The unconscious wants something the conscious mind rejects, so the desire is admitted in a form that gets past what is left of the censor.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: What does the case of the lonely person with thousands of followers demonstrate?
cards.answer: That attention and connection are different goods. Every metric a lonely person imagines would help was maxed out, and none of it touched the thing that was missing.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why do established friend groups stay closed even to someone who fits?
cards.answer: The barrier is history, not compatibility. The shared language was invented while you were elsewhere, and it cannot be joined retroactively however well you would suit the group.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why does the friendship recession get read as structural rather than personal?
cards.answer: Because connections rose while real friendships fell — the two curves diverge across every age group. Environments optimised for reach rather than depth explain a population-level pattern that individual failings cannot.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why is childhood friendship easy and adult friendship not?
cards.answer: Childhood supplies the whole formula for free — proximity plus hours. Adulthood requires schedules, values, emotional availability, trust and vulnerability to align at once, with nothing arranging that on your behalf.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: What is the characteristic waste of a signalling arms race?
cards.answer: Everyone spends more and nobody moves. The absolute cost of the signal rises while relative positions stay exactly where they were, because the signal only ever measured the gap.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: What makes the prisoner's dilemma a dilemma rather than a mistake?
cards.answer: Both players choose correctly given what the other might do, and both end up worse than if they had cooperated. The bad outcome is produced by rationality, not by error.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why does a bad standard like QWERTY survive?
cards.answer: Because the payoff comes from everyone doing the same thing, not from doing the best thing. A better standard loses to an entrenched one unless everybody switches at once.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why does repetition change the optimal strategy so completely?
cards.answer: Because future encounters give today’s behaviour a price. In a one-shot game defection has no consequence; repeated, it destroys the reputation that determines every subsequent round.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why look at the incentive structure before judging the person inside it?
cards.answer: Because the same structure produces the same behaviour from most people in it. A broken incentive explains the conduct better than character does, and it is the part that can be changed.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: How does a raise become part of the trap rather than an escape from it?
cards.answer: Expenses expand to fill it. After a few years the salary that felt like freedom is the minimum required to maintain the life built on it, so the increase bought no slack.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why is "I can't take risks, I have rent to pay" at 25 a self-fulfilling statement?
cards.answer: Acting on it builds the obligations that make it more true at 35 and more true again at 45. The sentence installs the conditions that justify it.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why is leaving a well-paid role costlier than losing the income?
cards.answer: Because the role became the identity. “I’m a senior manager at X” is the social self-concept and the basis of the professional relationships, so leaving forfeits those as well as the salary.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why must the two escape moves happen simultaneously?
cards.answer: Because either alone leaves the trap intact. Cutting obligations without building income means no route out; building income while inflating lifestyle means the new income is consumed before it can fund anything.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: What is the horn effect?
cards.answer: The halo running in reverse. A negative first impression generates assumptions of other negative traits by the same automatic extension, with no evidence for them either.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: What makes the Jeremy Meeks case a strong demonstration of the halo effect?
cards.answer: The context was maximally unfavourable. A mugshot arrives labelled with a conviction, and the attractiveness still overrode it at scale — so the extension is not merely absence of contrary information.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: Which two signals does the halo effect run on?
cards.answer: Physical attractiveness, generating assumptions of competence, intelligence and moral character; and projected confidence, generating assumptions of expertise, authority and trustworthiness.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: Why does a bias this crude survive rather than being trained out?
